text: Drive2Survive: Benchmarking Vision-Language-Action Autonomous Driving Models in Long-Tail Scenarios with Pre-Crash Precursor Metrics

Vision-language-action (VLA) models have become a trending approach to end-to-end driving [1], [2]. Unlike most robotics settings, autonomous driving is safety-critical: a single planning failure can be irreversible. Current VLA planning benchmarks have largely saturated ordinary urban driving [3] and grade models on average-case accuracy — displacement measures such as ADE and FDE — which reward typical behavior while the rare, long-tail interactions that produce real crashes stay underrepresented and under-weighted. Safety is also usually reported as a collision count, which scores a planner that keeps situations from ever turning dangerous the same as one that repeatedly creates its own near-misses and escapes them by chance. We are building an open protocol that evaluates VLA planners on long-tail scenarios and measures the pre-crash risk they accumulate, not only whether they crash. Scenarios come from the splits released with NAVSIM [4], built on nuPlan and OpenScene data [3], keeping our numbers comparable with published leaderboards. All planners run through one trajectory interface, and metrics are computed on the executed rollout.

We will evaluate four open-sourced state-of-the-art VLA planners, alongside the non-VLA agents shipped with NAVSIM — Transfuser, an ego-status MLP, constant velocity, and the privileged human agent. These four are the starting set for the Start-Up phase; the full proposal will extend the evaluation to a broader range of VLA planners.
AutoVLA [1] — unified autoregressive VLA with discrete action tokens, fast and slow reasoning modes, and reinforcement fine-tuning.
OpenDriveVLA [9] — open LLM backbone with 2D and 3D instance-aware visual tokens.
ORION [10] — QT-Former history aggregation with an LLM reasoner and generative planner, built for closed-loop rather than open-loop imitation.
Impromptu VLA [8] — open weights and open data, built around unstructured corner cases.

Besides crash rate, we will report surrogate measures standard in traffic safety research. For a lead vehicle at longitudinal gap Δx with length L and closing speed Δv, time-to-collision and the deceleration required to avoid a crash are
TTC(t) = Δx(t) - LΔv(t),          DRAC(t) = Δv(t)2Δx(t) - L(1)

both defined only while the gap is closing and zero otherwise; DRAC is the braking severity a plan forces on the ego vehicle [7]. The minimum of TTC over a rollout marks its worst instant but cannot separate a brief graze from sustained close following. Time-integrated TTC does, accumulating severity over duration against a threshold TTC* [5]:
TIT = tTTC* - TTC(t) Δt,          0 < TTC(t) ≤ TTC*(2)

The suite we report includes TTC, TIT, and DRAC but is not limited to them. Post-encroachment time [6] covers crossing conflicts that TTC's one-dimensional form misses, and progress and comfort bounds keep a planner from scoring well by crawling. TIT and DRAC are what separate planners that hold margin from those that survive on luck.
This project gives the community an open, reproducible way to measure how safely VLA driving models behave in the scenarios that matter, using accumulated pre-crash risk instead of a crash tally.
